records.content:
This Jupyter Book documents our end-to-end data engineering and machine learning pipeline built for the Introduction to Data Science course project.

While traditional bibliometric studies on arXiv rely solely on abstract-level metadata or hard-to-parse PDF files, this project constructs a structured dataset directly from full-text LaTeX source archives across all revision versions of each publication.

Our primary objective is to take raw, unstructured academic preprints from discovery through hierarchical document parsing to an automated Reference Matching Pipeline evaluated using Mean Reciprocal Rank at 5 (\text{MRR}@5).

records.content:
The project is structured into three cumulative milestones:

Milestone 1 — Data Crawling & Corpus Analysis:Discover papers within our assigned arXiv ID range, harvest paper and reference metadata via the arXiv API / OAI-PMH and Semantic Scholar, download every revision’s (v1 to vN) full-text LaTeX source bundle, and perform an exploratory statistical audit of the raw corpus.

Milestone 2 — Hierarchical Parsing & Standardization:Parse raw .tex and .bbl source files into a unified hierarchical document tree (elements and hierarchy), normalize mathematical and textual notation, convert raw \bibitem strings into standardized BibTeX records, and deduplicate content across paper revisions.

Milestone 3 — Reference Matching Pipeline:Design and evaluate a machine learning ranking pipeline—covering candidate generation, feature engineering, labeling, and modeling—to link unlabelled in-text/BibTeX citations to their ground-truth arXiv identifiers, scored via \text{MRR}@5.

records.content:
Our group’s assigned partition covers 15,000 arXiv publications( for a group of three with 5000 publications per student). Unlike static single-snapshot datasets, our corpus captures the complete longitudinal revision history of every assigned paper:

Multi-Version Coverage: Every available revision (v1, v2, ..., vN) is tracked independently to capture metadata updates, structural edits, and bibliography growth over time.

Full-Text LaTeX Sources: Raw .tar.gz source trees are extracted into versioned directories (latex_source_path) alongside inline \bibitem reference strings (raw_references).

Reproducible Analytics: All summary tables and visualizations in this book are dynamically compiled from our processed dataset during the Jupyter Book build process.

A comprehensive breakdown of the crawling architecture, rate-limit handling, and corpus quality audit is presented in Milestone 1 — Data Crawling.

arXiv Corpus Engineering & Reference Matching

Milestone 1: Data Crawling

Milestone 1: Crawler

Corpus Analysis — Milestone 1 (arXiv crawl)

Collect the arXiv publications assigned to our group — paper metadata, the LaTeX source of every version, and the reference lists — and profile the result. The corpus is the working input of Milestone 2 (hierarchical parsing) and Milestone 3 (reference matching), so the goal is a crawl that is complete, correctly organised and reproducible.

The crawler is a sequential pipeline. For each assigned arXiv ID it discovers the versions, fetches their metadata, downloads and cleans each version’s source, and extracts the raw bibliography. One JSON line per paper is appended to papers.jsonl; a paper that fails is written to failures.jsonl with the step and the error, and the run can be restarted at any time because finished IDs are skipped.generate IDs → probe versions → fetch metadata → download + extract source → extract references → papers.jsonl
                                                                                   └── on error → failures.jsonl

Tools and libraries: requests (HTTP), xml.etree.ElementTree (Atom parsing), tarfile (extraction), re (bibliography parsing), pandas / seaborn / matplotlib (analysis). OAI-PMH and the Kaggle snapshot were not needed: the IDs are assigned, so the arXiv API is enough to resolve them, and a repository-scale harvest is outside this milestone.

Politeness. Every request is followed by a 3-second pause (the arXiv API rule), a descriptive User-Agent (HCMUS-IntroDS-Crawler/1.0 (academic project)) identifies us, requests use timeouts, and one connection is used at a time.

Record structure (one line of papers.jsonl):arxiv_id
versions[]
  ├─ version              "v1", "v2", …
  ├─ metadata             title, authors[], abstract, categories[], submission_date
  ├─ latex_source_path    folder of the extracted source, or null when no source could be obtained
  └─ raw_references[]     raw \bibitem strings

What we have after this milestone:

A crawler that resolves each assigned ID into all of its versions and stores, per version, the metadata, the extracted LaTeX source folder and the raw references.

A corpus of 4,087 papers and 6,573 versions (1.61 versions per paper on average) out of 5,000 assigned IDs, i.e. a paper-level success rate of 81.7%. [TODO: confirm the assigned range — crawler.py is set to 2407.02839–2407.07838, but the sample dates shown in the analysis notebook (28 Aug 2024) cannot belong to a July 2024 ID. Use the range of the data the notebook actually analyses.]

A resumable run with a failure log, so no ID is lost silently.

A first quality profile of the corpus (02_corpus_analysis.ipynb): crawl completeness, missing fields, versions, references, categories and authors, meant to be executed at book-compilation time.

Every version is crawled. Versions are discovered by probing /abs/{id}v{n} until a 404, and each version is then downloaded individually, so revised papers keep their full history. Papers without obtainable source are kept with an empty record (latex_source_path = null) instead of being dropped.

Figures are removed to save space. After extraction, files with image extensions (.png, .jpg, .jpeg, .pdf, .eps, .gif, .bmp, .ps) are deleted; the figure environments and \includegraphics lines inside the .tex files are untouched, so Milestone 2 can still parse the document structure.

Safe extraction. Archive members are checked against path traversal before extraction, and the download goes to a temporary file that is always removed.

References are extracted from LaTeX as raw \bibitem strings (.bbl first, then thebibliography in .tex). They are not yet resolved to arXiv IDs.

Report. The statistics and figures are produced by a notebook that is meant to be executed when the Jupyter Book is compiled (execute_notebooks enabled in _config.yml), so they are not static screenshots.

The three largest primary categories are all computer science (cs.CV, cs.LG, cs.CL); physics and mathematics categories fill most of the rest of the top 12.

Throughput is bounded by the 3-second rule. For a paper with n versions the current pipeline waits up to 2n + 1 pauses (one per version probe, one for the metadata call, one per successful download), i.e. up to about 6n + 3 seconds. At the observed mean of 1.61 versions this is roughly 13 seconds per paper and about 14 hours of enforced waiting for 4,087 papers (estimate), before any transfer time.

Source formats. The extractor accepts only gzipped tar archives. Single-file sources and PDF-only submissions raise an error, the error is swallowed and the version is stored with null. As a result 14.68% of versions have no source — about five times the ~3% PDF-only rate that arXiv reports — and the log does not say why, so real PDF-only versions cannot be told apart from recoverable failures.

Bibliography formats. The \bibitem extractor cannot read biblatex output or a stand-alone .bib, and reads only the first .bbl it finds. This leaves 20.71% of versions without references (965 without source plus 396 with source).

Version dates are wrong. metadata.py stores the Atom <published> element, which the arXiv API defines as the date of version 1 whichever version is requested. Every version of a paper therefore has the same date: the revision span is 0 days for all multi-version papers and revised_dates cannot be filled correctly. The date of a specific version is in <updated>.

Failed IDs. 913 of the 5,000 assigned IDs are not in papers.jsonl. The notebook breaks them down by failing step and error message from failures.jsonl; IDs that do not exist or were removed are not crawler errors. [TODO: paste the failure breakdown once the notebook has run on the full data.]

Figure removal by deletion. Deleting a fixed list of image extensions leaves other non-source files (.sty, .cls, .bst, .bbl, …) in the corpus, whereas the project statement keeps only .tex and .bib. The archive size is not logged, so the size before removal cannot be reported yet.

How the performance numbers will be measured (auditable, on the Colab CPU-only testbed): wall-clock time per stage with time.perf_counter() written to a log; peak RAM with /usr/bin/time -v (or psutil); average RAM by sampling psutil.Process().memory_info().rss every few seconds in a background thread; maximum disk with du -sb taken before cleanup and at the end; final output size with du -sb data/. For the full system the runtime is the end-to-end wall time and the memory is the total of all processes.

In order of expected impact on the grade:

Add the Semantic Scholar crawl (required): for each paper call graph/v1/paper/arXiv:{id} with flat references.* fields, honour the rate limit, keep all references locally and mark those with externalIds.ArXiv. This yields the references table and the reference-scraping success rate, and covers versions whose LaTeX source is missing.

Fix the version dates: read <updated> per version and <arxiv:journal_ref> for venue, and re-fetch metadata only (no source download needed).

Switch discovery and download to the recommended endpoints: resolve versions with one API id_list request on the base ID (the returned vN suffix is the latest version) and download from export.arxiv.org/src/{id}vN instead of probing arxiv.org pages, which risks automatic blocking. Batching IDs into the API request leaves the downloads as the only paced step: about 6,573 × 3 s ≈ 5.5 h, roughly 2.6× faster than now (estimate).

Make the source step robust and observable: handle non-tar sources, retry transient errors, and store a source_status / reason per version so that PDF-only, withdrawn and failed downloads are distinguishable; then re-run the failed IDs.

Extract only .tex and .bib from the archive (never writing other files) and record archive and extracted sizes; fix the 429/503 branch of the version probe so that a rate-limited version is retried instead of skipped.

Reproducibility: add README.md and requirements.txt to the code repository and make sure the notebook’s helper (utils/build_summary.py) is in it.

Measure running time and memory on Colab and fill in the KPI table.

The crawler already produces a usable corpus of 4,087 papers and 6,573 versions with metadata, source folders and raw references, and a notebook that profiles its quality. The analysis also shows what is still missing before the corpus is a sound base for Milestones 2 and 3: correct per-version dates, the Semantic Scholar reference metadata and the venue, a more complete source download (14.68% of versions are empty), and measured performance figures. Closing these gaps is the work of the next iteration; none of them needs the whole crawl to be repeated from scratch, except the source download for the versions that failed.

This notebook profiles the corpus produced by the crawler in src/. It belongs to the Milestone 1 report and is meant to be re-executed when the Jupyter Book is compiled, so that every table and figure is generated from the crawled data and not pasted as a screenshot.

What is analysed

Scope — the assigned ID range, how many papers and versions were crawled, and which IDs failed.

Record structure — one JSON object per paper in papers.jsonl, flattened into two summary tables: papers_summary (one row per paper) and versions_summary (one row per version). It is also compared with the papers / references tables required by the project statement.

Data quality — value types, missing fields, crawl completeness and what the corpus stores on disk.

Content statistics — versions per paper, references per paper, categories and authors.

Each section ends with Findings, and the last section lists the actions that follow for Milestones 2 (parsing) and 3 (matching).

# You only have to run this to generate `summary/` folder from crawled data( which we have provided for you)
# import json
# from pathlib import Path

# import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
# import pandas as pd
# import seaborn as sns

# from utils.build_summary import build_book_summaries

# sns.set_theme(style="whitegrid", palette="muted")

# # Paths are relative to this notebook. The data folder is NOT part of the code repository.
# DATA_DIR = Path("../data")
# SUMMARY_DIR = DATA_DIR / "summary"

# build_book_summaries(DATA_DIR, SUMMARY_DIR)



import json
from pathlib import Path

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import pandas as pd
import seaborn as sns

sns.set_theme(style="whitegrid", palette="muted")

# Only the lightweight summary folder is required to compile the book
SUMMARY_DIR = Path("../data/summary")

df_papers = pd.read_parquet(SUMMARY_DIR / "papers_summary.parquet")
df_versions = pd.read_parquet(SUMMARY_DIR / "versions_summary.parquet")
with open(SUMMARY_DIR / "crawl_meta.json", "r", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    crawl_meta = json.load(f)

n_assigned = crawl_meta["n_assigned"]
n_crawled = crawl_meta["n_crawled"]
n_failed = crawl_meta["n_failed"]
n_untracked = crawl_meta["n_untracked"]

scope = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "Metric": [
            "First ID",
            "Last ID",
            "Assigned IDs",
            "Papers crawled (in papers.jsonl)",
            "Versions crawled",
            "Failed IDs (logged in failures.jsonl)",
            "Never attempted / not logged",
            "Paper-level success rate (%)",
        ],
        "Value": [
            crawl_meta["first_id"],
            crawl_meta["last_id"],
            f"{n_assigned:,}",
            f"{n_crawled:,}",
            f"{crawl_meta['n_versions_crawled']:,}",
            f"{n_failed:,}",
            f"{n_untracked:,}",
            f"{n_crawled / n_assigned * 100:.2f}",
        ],
    }
)
display(scope)

if crawl_meta.get("failed_by_step"):
    print("Failed IDs by crawler step")
    display(
        pd.Series(crawl_meta["failed_by_step"], name="failed_ids")
        .rename_axis("step")
        .to_frame()
    )
    print("Most frequent error messages (IDs normalised)")
    display(
        pd.Series(crawl_meta["failed_by_error"], name="failed_ids")
        .rename_axis("error")
        .to_frame()
    )











How to read the table

Assigned IDs is the number of IDs written to arxiv_ids.txt by the ID generator; Papers crawled are the IDs that reached papers.jsonl; Failed IDs come from failures.jsonl.

The step table shows where a paper was lost (version probing, metadata call, or an unexpected error) and the error table shows why. IDs that fail at the probing step with “No versions found” are IDs that do not exist or were removed — these are not crawler bugs.

Never attempted / not logged should be 0. If it is not, the run was interrupted or an error escaped the logger; run the crawler again (it resumes from papers.jsonl).

The success rate is measured per paper. Missing LaTeX sources inside a paper that was crawled are audited separately in Crawl completeness.

Extra fields we keep (abstract, categories, latex_source_path, raw_references) are harmless and useful for Milestone 2, but they do not replace the required columns above.

What the next cell does. Before analysing anything, it checks that the tables loaded from Parquet have the types the later cells rely on:

it lists every column of the version table that contains missing values (columns with no missing values are hidden);

for four columns — metadata.categories, metadata.submission_date, num_categories and submission_dt — it prints which Python types occur and two example values.

What we expect to see. Only latex_source_path should have missing values. metadata.categories should be an array, the raw date an ISO-8601 string, and the derived submission_dt a timezone-aware UTC timestamp, so dates can be compared and subtracted safely.

print("=== Missing values in original version-level data ===")
display(
    df_versions.isna()
    .sum()
    .sort_values(ascending=False)
    .to_frame("missing_count")
    .query("missing_count > 0")
)


cols = [
    "metadata.categories",
    "metadata.submission_date",
    "num_categories",
    "submission_dt"
]

for col in cols:
    print(f"\n{col}")
    print("Data types:")
    print(df_versions[col].map(type).value_counts().head())
    print("Examples:")
    print(df_versions[col].head(2).tolist())







Findings

The only column with missing values is latex_source_path (965 of 6,573 versions). This is a crawl gap rather than a schema problem and is audited in the next section.

Every column holds a single type (no mixed str / float values), so no cleaning step is needed before the analysis.

metadata.categories is a NumPy array after the Parquet round trip, so category counts need explode() or the primary_category column of the paper table.

Look at the two example dates: the first two rows look like two versions of the same paper, yet they carry the same timestamp. This is not a formatting issue — it is the date problem analysed in Version and revision analysis.

Purpose of this check. For every crawled version, count which required parts are absent: the metadata fields (title, categories, submission date), the LaTeX source, and the extracted bibliography. Percentages are relative to all crawled versions.

What we should discover

Metadata should be complete, because it comes from the arXiv API and every paper has it.

Only a small share of versions without source. The project statement says arXiv provides source for about 97% of submissions, so we should expect roughly 3% PDF-only versions.

Some versions that have source but produce no references — a signal of the limits of our \bibitem extractor.

# Identify valid source paths directly from latex_source_path
valid_source_mask = (
    df_versions["latex_source_path"].notna() 
    & (df_versions["latex_source_path"].astype(str).str.strip() != "")
)

audit_metrics = {
    "Missing Title": df_versions["metadata.title"].isna().sum(),
    "Empty Categories": (df_versions["num_categories"] == 0).sum(),
    "Missing Submission Date": df_versions["submission_dt"].isna().sum(),
    "Missing LaTeX Source Path (PDF-only / Withdrawn)": (~valid_source_mask).sum(),
    "Has Source Path, But 0 Extracted \\bibitem Refs": (valid_source_mask & (df_versions["num_raw_refs"] == 0)).sum(),
    "Total Versions with 0 Extracted \\bibitem Refs": (df_versions["num_raw_refs"] == 0).sum(),
}

audit_df = pd.DataFrame([
    {
        "Metric / Field Check": k,
        "Affected Versions": int(v),
        "Percentage (%)": round(v / len(df_versions) * 100, 2),
    }
    for k, v in audit_metrics.items()
])
display(audit_df)



Findings

Metadata is complete. Missing Title, Empty Categories and Missing Submission Date are all 0 because these fields come straight from the arXiv API. Complete does not mean correct: see the date problem below.

965 versions (14.68%) have no LaTeX source. The table labels them “PDF-only / Withdrawn”, but that is an assumption. The crawler catches every error of the download step, prints a warning and stores null, so a genuine PDF-only submission, a withdrawn paper, a timeout and a source that is not a .tar.gz (for example a single gzipped .tex file) all look identical. Since the expected PDF-only rate is about 3%, a rate near five times higher suggests that a large part of these versions are recoverable crawl failures and not missing data.

396 versions (6.02%) have a source but no extracted reference. Plausible causes: a .bib file without a shipped .bbl, biblatex output (no thebibliography environment), a bibliography \input from another file, or a paper without references. The extractor also reads only the first .bbl it finds.

1,361 versions (20.71%) have zero extracted references. This is exactly 965 + 396: a version without source always has an empty reference list, so the two causes add up.

Impact. More than one version in five cannot contribute to the references table and 14.68% cannot be parsed in Milestone 2. Improving the source step first is the best return on effort because it feeds both numbers. For references, Semantic Scholar does not depend on LaTeX and can cover versions whose source is missing.

# The same audit at paper level: how many *papers* are affected, not only versions?
paper_audit = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "Check": [
            "Papers with no LaTeX source in any version",
            "Papers whose latest version has 0 extracted references",
        ],
        "Papers": [
            int((df_papers["versions_with_source"] == 0).sum()),
            int((df_papers["latest_refs"] == 0).sum()),
        ],
    }
)
paper_audit["Percentage (%)"] = (paper_audit["Papers"] / len(df_papers) * 100).round(2)
display(paper_audit)

records.content:
The project statement keeps only .tex and .bib files in the corpus (figure binaries and other files must never enter it). The next cell inventories data/raw by file extension, reports the corpus size, and counts how much is not .tex / .bib.

INVENTORY_FILE = SUMMARY_DIR / "corpus_inventory.parquet"

if INVENTORY_FILE.exists():
    by_ext = pd.read_parquet(INVENTORY_FILE).set_index("extension")
    n_versions_with_source = int(df_versions["latex_source_path"].notna().sum())
    total_bytes = int(by_ext["total_bytes"].sum())
    non_source_bytes = int(
        by_ext.loc[~by_ext.index.isin([".tex", ".bib"]), "total_bytes"].sum()
    )

    by_ext["share_of_bytes_%"] = (by_ext["total_bytes"] / total_bytes * 100).round(2)

    print(f"Corpus size on disk (after figure removal): {total_bytes / 1e6:,.1f} MB")
    print(f"Average per crawled paper:                  {total_bytes / len(df_papers) / 1e3:,.1f} kB")
    print(f"Average per version with source:            {total_bytes / n_versions_with_source / 1e3:,.1f} kB")
    print(f"Bytes in files other than .tex/.bib:        {non_source_bytes / total_bytes:.1%}")
    display(by_ext.head(10))

    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.5))
    top = by_ext.head(8)
    sns.barplot(x=top["total_bytes"] / 1e6, y=top.index, ax=ax, color="slategray")
    ax.set_title("Corpus size by file extension (top 8)")
    ax.set_xlabel("Size (MB)")
    ax.set_ylabel("Extension")
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()
else:
    print("No saved inventory found: skipping the on-disk analysis.")



How to read it. In a corpus that follows the statement, .tex and .bib should account for essentially all files. Any other extension (.sty, .cls, .bst, .bbl, .svg, .tikz, …) means the cleaning step deleted a fixed list of image extensions instead of extracting only the wanted file types, so non-figure files are still stored.

Not measured here: the size before figure removal. The crawler deletes the downloaded archive and does not record its size, so the “average paper size in bytes before and after removing figures” required by the report must be measured separately (for instance by re-downloading a random sample of papers and recording the archive size and the extracted .tex + .bib size).

print("=== Summary Statistics Across Unique Papers ===")
display(
    df_papers[["num_versions", "num_authors", "abstract_words", "latest_refs", "revision_span_days"]]
    .describe(percentiles=[0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 0.90, 0.99])
    .T.round(2)
)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4.5))

# Plot 1: Number of Versions per Paper
v_counts = df_papers["num_versions"].value_counts().sort_index()
sns.barplot(x=v_counts.index, y=v_counts.values, ax=axes[0], color="steelblue")
axes[0].set_title("Distribution of Paper Versions (v1 to vN)")
axes[0].set_xlabel("Total Versions per Paper")
axes[0].set_ylabel("Number of Papers")

# Plot 2: Revision span in days (papers with >= 2 versions)
multi_v = df_papers[df_papers["num_versions"] >= 2]
span = multi_v["revision_span_days"].dropna()
if span.max() == 0:
    # Every version carries the v1 date, so the span is meaningless (see the findings below).
    axes[1].text(
        0.5, 0.5,
        "All revision spans are 0 days\n(data issue: every version stores the v1 date)",
        ha="center", va="center", transform=axes[1].transAxes,
    )
    axes[1].set_axis_off()
else:
    sns.histplot(span, bins=25, kde=True, ax=axes[1], color="teal")
    axes[1].set_xlabel("Revision Span (Days)")
    axes[1].set_ylabel("Number of Papers")
axes[1].set_title("Time Span Between v1 and Latest Version (Multi-Version Papers)")

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()







# Exact share of papers per number of versions (the bars above, as numbers)
share = df_papers["num_versions"].value_counts(normalize=True).sort_index().mul(100).round(1)
display(share.to_frame("share_of_papers_%").T)

# Date check using `distinct_dates` from papers_summary.parquet
multi_df = df_papers[df_papers["crawled_versions"] >= 2]
if not multi_df.empty:
    same_date = int((multi_df["distinct_dates"] == 1).sum())
    print(f"Multi-version papers: {len(multi_df):,}")
    print(f"... whose versions ALL share one submission_date: {same_date:,} ({same_date / len(multi_df):.1%})")

Findings

Most papers are never revised. The median is 1 version; 75% of papers have at most 2 versions, 90% at most 3 and 99% at most 5 (maximum 10). The mean is 1.61, so the 4,087 papers expand to 6,573 versions: the every-version requirement costs on average 1.6 source downloads per paper.

Roughly 1,150 papers have exactly two versions and about 350 have three (exact shares in the table above); only about 170 papers have four or more.

The right-hand panel is not valid yet. Every multi-version paper (about 1,700 papers) shows a revision span of exactly 0 days, and the date check confirms that all versions of a paper share one timestamp. Real revisions are separated by days or months, so this is a data-collection bug, not a property of the corpus. metadata.py stores the Atom <published> element, which the arXiv API defines as the submission date of version 1 whatever version is requested; the date of the requested version is in <updated>. As a result revised_dates — a required column of the papers table — is wrong for every revised paper.

Fix: read <updated> for each version (and <arxiv:journal_ref> for the venue, which is also still missing) and re-fetch the metadata only. This takes one batched API request per roughly 100 versions and does not require downloading any source again. The plot above fills in automatically once the data is corrected.

Findings — categories (left panel)

Of the twelve most frequent primary categories, five belong to computer science (cs.CV, cs.LG, cs.CL, cs.RO, cs.CR), four to physics (quant-ph, hep-ph, cond-mat.mtrl-sci, astro-ph.GA), two to mathematics (math.AP, math.CO) and one to electrical engineering and systems science (eess.SP).

Machine-learning subfields dominate: cs.CV is the single largest category, followed by cs.LG and cs.CL.

The distribution has a long tail: the twelve categories above cover only a minority of the papers (the exact share is printed above), so most of the corpus is spread over many small categories. The corpus is a contiguous ID range from one period, not a random sample of arXiv, so these shares should not be generalised to arXiv as a whole.

Why it matters. Physics, mathematics and computer science use different bibliography tooling and conventions. Testing whether the 396 “source but no references” versions concentrate in particular categories is a cheap first step in Milestone 2 (hypothesis, not yet verified).

Findings — authors (right panel, clipped at the 99th percentile = 29 authors)

The distribution is right-skewed: median 3 authors, 75% of papers have at most 5 and 90% at most 8. The mean (6.59) is pulled up by a few very large collaborations (maximum 1,140 authors).

The most common team size is 3 authors; single-author papers are about 12% of the corpus.

Why it matters. A few papers carry hundreds of authors, which makes author lists a weak and expensive matching key for such papers in Milestone 3. Title and arXiv ID are better primary keys; authors are best used as a secondary signal.
